name: Sky Tower
label: Sky Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Victoria Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Waiatarau / Victoria Park' (way/7977840): middle (535 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9692605: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sky Tower' (57 m across).
notes: The tallest structure in the Southern Hemisphere, visible across the city.

text.description:
The Sky Tower is Auckland's tall landmark, rising 328 metres from ground level to the top of the mast. That makes it the second-tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere. It stands at the corner of Victoria and Federal Streets in the CBD, as part of the SkyCity complex, and opened on 3 August 1997 after two years and nine months of building. The slim concrete shaft carries the observation decks and restaurants near the top, so the outline is easy to recognise even in a small phone frame.

The best photo is of the tower from outside, because you can't photograph it from inside it. Victoria Park works well. The tower rises above the green lawns, with the city's high-rises and the harbour side of the CBD around it. The grass gives you a calm foreground and the tower gives the picture a clear centre.

Hold the phone upright, since the tower is much taller than it is wide. Leave a little space above the mast so the tip isn't clipped. If you have time, two other spots are worth a look: Wynyard Crossing, for the tower as the main element of the skyline from the Viaduct side, and Federal Street, for a street-level view, often reflected in nearby glass. The tower is also lit up for charities and causes, and for New Year fireworks, so an evening visit can give a very different picture.
text.geographic_location: The Sky Tower is in the middle of Auckland's CBD, at the corner of Victoria and Federal Streets, as part of the SkyCity complex. Victoria Park, where the photo is taken, lies to the west of it, also in the CBD.
text.directions_text: Victoria Park is in the CBD and easy to reach on foot. Federal Street is on the way if you want a second, street-level photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), held upright, to take in the tower with the lawns below it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for more grass and sky, or zoom to 2x-3x (if your phone has a telephoto) to fill the frame with the shaft and the pod.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Victoria Park. The tower rises above the green lawns of the park, with the city's high-rises and the harbour side of the CBD around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the shaft up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Put lawn or a tree in the lower third and leave a little space above the mast. For other angles, try Wynyard Crossing for the skyline from the Viaduct side, or Federal Street for the tower reflected in glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pod near the top of the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail. If you shoot at dusk, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon often gives softer light on the tower and the lawns. Dusk is a good time to catch the tower lit up.

text.access_note: Victoria Park is a public park, but going up the tower or joining any activities there is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Victoria Park is an open public park that can be entered without a ticket.
Late afternoon usually gives softer light for photographing the tower.
The tower is likely to fit in an upright 1x frame from the park, and 2x-3x zoom will fill the frame with the shaft and pod.
Dusk is a good time to catch the tower lit up.
Victoria Park is easy to reach on foot.

name: Maungawhau / Mount Eden
label: Mount Eden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maungawhau / Mount Eden' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/258927248: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mount Eden'.
notes: The highest natural point in the city, with a volcanic crater and 360° views.

text.description:
Maungawhau / Mount Eden is a grassy volcanic cone, and at 196 metres it is the highest natural point on the Auckland isthmus. That height is why it makes such a good photo spot. You get a deep, bowl-shaped crater close at hand, with the city skyline and the Sky Tower rising behind it. The crater is about 50 metres deep, and its smooth green sides give the foreground a clean, simple shape.

The name means 'mountain of the whau tree'. The mountain was once an important Māori fortified settlement, and the terraces and storage pits on the upper slopes are still protected. Boardwalks around the crater rim were opened in 2020 to look after them, so please stay on the boardwalk. The summit road has been closed to most vehicles since 2011.

For the classic shot, use the boardwalk platform closest to the access road. Reviewers say it gives the best view of the city and the Sky Tower, with the crater bowl in front. Include a strip of the grass in the bottom of the frame to give the picture depth. The summit is open and exposed, so allow a minute or two to line things up. If the platform is busy, wait for a gap rather than shooting over people's shoulders. For a quieter picture of the cone itself, try Mount Eden Road, which shows the green slopes rising above the street without the summit crowds.
text.geographic_location: Maungawhau / Mount Eden sits in the suburb of Mount Eden, on the Auckland isthmus. The summit looks out over the whole city.
text.directions_text: Head to Mount Eden by whatever route suits you and check current access for the final stretch. The summit road is closed to most vehicles, so expect to finish the last stretch on foot up to the summit boardwalk. Check current access on the day before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole crater bowl and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the city. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Sky Tower and the city towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the crater's grassy bowl fills the foreground, with the Auckland skyline and Sky Tower behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line. Keep the crater rim as a curve leading towards the skyline, and put the Sky Tower on one of the vertical lines rather than in the middle. For a quieter alternative, take a 1x or 2x shot of the green cone from Mount Eden Road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Sky Tower or the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, use night mode and rest your elbows on the rail to keep the phone steady. Wait for the countdown to finish before moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or sunrise, which several guides single out for photos.

text.access_note: The summit boardwalk is free and open to the public, but vehicle access to the top is restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Karangahape Road
label: Karangahape Road
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karangahape Road' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Karangahape Road and Pitt Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9690719: large area 'Karangahape Road' (994 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Auckland's colourful street of street art, shops and nightlife.

text.description:
Karangahape Road, usually just called K' Road, is one of Auckland's main streets. It follows a ridge along the southern edge of the city centre, so a photo along it shows the street climbing away between older buildings. The classic view is from the corner looking west. The historic H B Building stands on one side and the Naval and Family Hotel on the other, with the Family Bar sign far down the street. Photos from this same corner appear in 1909 postcard views, so you are shooting a very old composition.

The road is older than Queen Street. Māori used the ridge as a walking route long before Europeans arrived, and the ridge was known as Te Ara o Karangahape, 'The Path of Karangahape'. The meaning of the name itself is uncertain. From about 1900 to the early 1960s it was Auckland's busiest shopping street. In 1935 the whole street was lit with lights under the shop awnings, known as the 'Great White Way'. Today it is known for off-beat cafes and boutique shops.

For a phone photo, wait for a gap in the traffic and people, and look for the lines of the old facades leading your eye up the street. If the signs or shopfronts are the main interest, step back and use the buildings as a frame. Some parts are busy, and the area has people sleeping rough, so be thoughtful when people are in your shot. Building work for the new City Rail Link station near the Upper Queen Street end may change some views, so check on site.
text.geographic_location: Karangahape Road runs west to east along a ridge at the southern edge of Auckland's city centre, crossing Queen Street's line at right angles. It runs from Ponsonby Road in the west to Grafton Bridge in the east.
text.directions_text: Start from Queen Street in the city centre and head south, uphill, towards the ridge. If you are coming from further out, walk to the corner of Karangahape Road and Pitt Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want both rows of buildings and more sky, but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the distant Family Bar sign closer and squeeze the street together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Karangahape Road and Pitt Street (corner, looking west along the strip). The street running away up the ridge, framed by the historic H B Building on one side and the Naval and Family Hotel on the other, with the Family Bar sign in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the street's centre line near the middle, with the two buildings as framing on either side. Tap the far end of the street to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright. For a different view, St Kevin's Arcade has heritage architecture, vintage signs and mural-covered walls. Grafton Bridge shows the city skyline and its concrete arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Wait for a quiet moment so cars and people don't cover the buildings. If you want a shot with people in it, take a few quick Live Photos or a short burst and choose the best one afterwards. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the building details. Late afternoon to evening can be good for lit signs and shopfronts, though the low sun may be in front of you when looking west.

text.access_note: This is an ordinary city street that you can photograph from the pavement; shops and venues along it have their own rules, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside anywhere.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west, the low evening sun may be in front of the camera.
Late afternoon to evening is a good time for lit signs and shopfronts.
Karangahape Road is an open public street that can be photographed from the pavement without a ticket.
Gridlines and a quiet moment between traffic and people help to keep the street composition tidy.

name: Wynyard Quarter
label: Wynyard Quarter
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wynyard Crossing' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wynyard Crossing Bridge' (way/429009401): middle (110 m across); moved 40 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/440089487: the OpenStreetMap point 'Wynyard Quarter'.
notes: Waterfront precinct with the converted silos and harbour views.

text.description:
Wynyard Quarter is a stretch of reclaimed land on the Waitematā Harbour, at the western edge of the Auckland waterfront. Its last section, Wynyard Wharf, was finished around 1930, and for decades it was mostly port land and fuel tanks, which is why many locals still call it the Tank Farm. Since 2011 the eastern part has been open to the public as a mix of restaurants, walkways and open space, including Silo Park, where old industrial structures now sit among lawns and event areas. Working fishing boats and ferries still use the docks, so the waterfront feels lived-in rather than polished.

The best single view is from Wynyard Crossing, the bridge over the marina. From midspan you can look toward the colourful silos, with the marina in front and the city skyline behind. The bridge's modern steel structure gives you a natural frame, and its railings make good leading lines. If a tall yacht comes through, the bridge swings open, which makes for a lively shot but can briefly stop you crossing, so allow a few spare minutes. Crossing on foot is free.

If you have time afterwards, walk on to Silo Park for a close-up of the silos, or to the Auckland Fish Market to photograph boats coming and going. Conditions change, so check current details before you go.
text.geographic_location: Wynyard Quarter is on the western edge of Auckland's waterfront, north of Freemans Bay and west of the Viaduct Basin, on the Waitematā Harbour.
text.directions_text: Head for the Viaduct Basin on the western side of the city waterfront; Wynyard Crossing is the bridge over the marina that leads across to the Quarter. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the bridge structure, the marina and the skyline together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the silos. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the silos or a single boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wynyard Crossing (midspan, looking across the marina toward Silo Park). The silos and marina framed by the bridge's modern steel structure, with the city skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the bridge's steel lines to lead the eye toward the silos. Keep the horizon level and keep the railings straight. If a tall yacht is due, wait for the bridge to swing for a more dynamic shot. For a second option, try Silo Park for the silos in the foreground with the harbour beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the silos to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After the sun has gone, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time to aim for.

text.access_note: Wynyard Crossing and the waterfront paths are open public space and free to walk on, but the bridge can lift for tall boats, so check current conditions before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The bridge can briefly stop pedestrians crossing when it swings open (from the notes; timings are not given).
Wynyard Crossing is the bridge linking the Viaduct Basin side to Wynyard Quarter.
Main part of Wynyard Quarter is about 7 minutes on foot from the stand-here point (calculated from distance).
Resting your elbows on the railing helps steady a phone for night shots.

name: Auckland War Memorial Museum
label: Auckland Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cenotaph' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cenotaph Road' (way/44404088): point nearest the subject (165 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23906678: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Auckland War Memorial Museum' (153 m across).
notes: Neoclassical museum on a hill in the Domain, with a Māori and Pacific collection.

text.description:
Auckland War Memorial Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira in Māori) is a pale, temple-like building on top of Observatory Hill in the Auckland Domain, just outside the city centre. It was built as a museum and a memorial to those lost in the First World War. Building began in 1925 and it opened in 1929. The design is Greco-Roman, and the walls are mostly Portland stone with carved reliefs of the armed forces by Richard Gross. Hilltop sites were chosen partly for the view over the Waitematā Harbour, and that view is why this spot works so well.

The best photo is taken from the Cenotaph on the forecourt. The memorial sits in the foreground, the big museum building rises behind it, and the harbour opens out toward Rangitoto Island. Because the cenotaph is a place of remembrance, keep your framing respectful and avoid posed or playful shots right at the memorial. For a different picture, walk to the museum's columns and shoot the facade framed between them, with the sloping lawn and trees leading toward the city. A third option is to look back at the building from Domain Drive with the Robert Burns Statue in front. That view comes from an old photo record, so check on the ground that it still works.

If you want to go inside, check the official site before you go for opening times and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: In the Auckland Domain, on the summit of Observatory Hill, a short distance from the Auckland city centre. The museum overlooks the Waitematā Harbour.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so head for the Auckland Domain, just outside the city centre. Once you reach the museum, walk to the forecourt in front of the building, where the Cenotaph stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the cenotaph and the whole museum in one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for Rangitoto in the distance or for details of the carved reliefs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the museum, on the forecourt). The war memorial in the foreground with the museum behind it, and a wide view across the harbour toward Rangitoto Island.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the museum's columns and the cenotaph upright, so the buildings don't lean. Crouch slightly to put the cenotaph against the building. Try a second picture facing the harbour, using the telephoto to bring Rangitoto closer. If you want a different angle, the museum's columns frame the facade with the lawn leading toward the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the walls keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out. For the harbour view, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly and level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone. Light conditions are best judged on the day, so check the sky and the shadows on the facade as you arrive.

text.access_note: The Domain is open to the public, but museum opening hours, ticketing and any photography rules inside should be checked on the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter pale stone buildings.
Rangitoto will look small at the default lens (1x), so the telephoto helps.
Pale stone can look washed out unless the exposure is lowered slightly.
The Domain Drive view may differ from the historical photo, so it should be checked on the ground.

name: Britomart Transport Centre
label: Britomart
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lower Queen Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lower Queen Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/940237256: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Waitematā' (364 m across).
notes: Historic railway terminus area with restored heritage buildings.

text.description: Waitematā Station, still labelled Britomart on some maps, is the underground rail station at the foot of Queen Street, with the main ferry terminal just across Quay Street. The part worth photographing is above ground: the restored Edwardian facade of the Chief Post Office, which holds the station's main entrance. The post office dates from 1912, and Auckland City Council bought the old building in 1995 as part of the plan for a new transport centre. The station opened to passengers on 7 July 2003. Sir Edmund Hillary performed the official opening later that month. The old building and the busy modern interchange make a good contrast, and the carved, symmetrical frontage gives a strong, tidy picture. For the classic shot, stand on Lower Queen Street opposite the building and frame the whole facade, with the entrance near the middle. If you want a wider view of the station frontage, Te Komititanga, with its Tūhono light artwork in front of the building, is a good alternative. Takutai Square, at the eastern entrance, is quieter and has a lawn and fountain in the foreground. People will be walking in and out all day, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the Auckland city centre, at the bottom of Queen Street where it meets the waterfront. The ferry terminal is just across Quay Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the foot of Queen Street in central Auckland. The station building is at the waterfront end, opposite the ferry terminal. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are too close to fit it in. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out carved details or the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lower Queen Street (opposite the Chief Post Office facade, near the station entrance). The grand Edwardian facade of the restored Chief Post Office building that houses the station's main entrance. The station lies to the south-east of this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the vertical edges stay straight. Keep the entrance near the centre and include a little pavement for scale. For a different view, try Te Komititanga for a wider shot of the station frontage with the Tūhono light artwork, or Takutai Square for a quieter angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone level, because tilting makes the building lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day and choose the moment when the front is evenly lit.

text.access_note: The facade is best seen from Lower Queen Street. Check the official site before you go if you want to go inside the station or use any particular entrance.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the exposure slightly lower helps retain detail in the stonework when the sky is bright.

name: Viaduct Harbour
label: Viaduct Harbour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wynyard Crossing' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wynyard Crossing Bridge' (way/429009401): middle (110 m across); moved 40 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4092147644: the OpenStreetMap point 'Viaduct Harbour'.
notes: Marina lined with bars and restaurants, with superyachts and the city skyline.

text.description:
Viaduct Harbour is a former working harbour on the Auckland waterfront, now lined with apartments, offices and restaurants. It was once known as Viaduct Basin and was laid out on the lines of the basins common in London. For much of the 20th century it was the centre of Auckland's fishing industry, and a mechanical bridge was raised to let the fishing boats in. It later became the hub of the 2000 America's Cup. That mix of old harbour layout and modern buildings is what makes it photograph so well: yachts packed into the basin, glass-fronted buildings around the edge and the city rising behind.

The best view for this map is from Wynyard Crossing, a bridge to the north. From there you look south across the marina and the yachts, with the Sky Tower and the city skyline behind. A tourism guide calls it the best waterfront photo spot in the area. Wynyard Crossing is a swing bridge that opens for tall vessels, and it frames the marina and the Silo Park silos especially well when it is mid-lift. A signal sounds before it moves, so keep your phone ready. If the bridge is busy, the ANZ Viaduct Events Centre gives a similar view of the marina and the harbour frontage with the skyline behind. Keep your phone low and steady near the water, and watch your footing on the bridge.
text.geographic_location: Viaduct Harbour is on the Auckland waterfront at the edge of the CBD, beside Freemans Bay and next to Wynyard Quarter.
text.directions_text: Head for the Auckland CBD waterfront and aim for Viaduct Harbour. Wynyard Crossing is on the northern side of the basin, so walk north along the water's edge to reach it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the yachts with the Sky Tower behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the basin and the sky in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Sky Tower or a single yacht.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wynyard Crossing. The marina and the yachts in the basin, with the Sky Tower and CBD skyline rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the line of yachts along the lower third, with the Sky Tower sitting off-centre against the sky. Keep the phone level so the masts and buildings stay upright. If the swing bridge starts to lift for a passing vessel, take a few shots, as the lifting bridge adds interest to the frame. As an alternative, the ANZ Viaduct Events Centre shows the marina and harbour frontage with the skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yachts to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo while the bridge moves, then choose the best frame afterwards. Use night mode after dark, and brace your elbows on the rail to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the bridge is mid-lift for a passing vessel, if you can catch it. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and buildings, and the lights come on in the evening.

text.access_note: The bridge opens for tall vessels, so the view can be interrupted.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and buildings.
The city lights come on in the evening, which suits night mode.
Wynyard Crossing is on the northern side of the basin and can be reached by walking north along the water's edge.
Viaduct Harbour is next to Wynyard Quarter and Freemans Bay, with Wynyard Crossing just north of the basin.

name: Auckland Harbour Bridge
label: Harbour Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stokes Point Reserve' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stokes Point Reserve / Te Onewa Pā' (relation/10976226): middle (290 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/302049182: large area 'Auckland Harbour Bridge' (1625 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Steel arch bridge across the Waitematā Harbour.

text.description:
The Auckland Harbour Bridge carries the Northern Motorway across the Waitematā Harbour, linking St Marys Bay on the city side with Northcote on the North Shore. The original four lanes opened in 1959. Two more lanes were added to each side in 1968–1969. The whole bridge is 1,020 m long, and its main span rises about 43 m above high water so that ships can pass underneath.

The best-value phone view is from Stokes Point Reserve, a park on the north side almost directly beneath the bridge. Looking up, you see the steelwork and the piers marching away, and the city skyline sits across the water beyond. The angle gives a real sense of scale and is less common than the wide view from the wharf. A memorial plaque to men killed during construction is recorded underneath the bridge at the Northcote end, so be respectful if you come across it.

Expect a working, industrial feel rather than a polished viewpoint. The reserve is reported as windy, noisy and dusty, with limited parking and no public toilets. Hold your phone with both hands, wipe the lens before you start, and don't linger near the road. If you want a wider, calmer view, the wharf at Northcote Point shows the bridge with the skyline behind it.
text.geographic_location: On the North Shore side of the Waitematā Harbour, beneath the north end of the bridge near Northcote.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near this spot, so head for Northcote, the North Shore end of the bridge, and check local transport options, or take a taxi. Parking at the reserve is limited, so a drop-off may be easier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full upward sweep of the bridge, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer composition. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the city skyline closer between the piers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Stokes Point Reserve (north side, directly beneath the bridge). A close-up, upward perspective of the bridge's structure with the city skyline visible across the water. The bridge lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone upwards and use the gridlines to keep the piers and edges straight. Let the lines of the deck lead the eye towards the skyline. For a different view, the wharf at Northcote Point gives a wide shot with the bridge framing the city, and Westhaven Promenade offers yachts in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steelwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps some colour. In the wind, hold the phone with both hands and take a few frames of each shot to make sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the steelwork. At dusk, try night mode with your elbows tucked in or the phone resting on a solid surface.

text.access_note: Stokes Point Reserve is a public park beneath the bridge, but the bridge itself is a motorway, so photograph from the park and check the official site before you go for any access changes.

photo.artist: Ingolfson at English Wikipedia (Original text: Uploader.)

name: Auckland Art Gallery
label: Auckland Art Gallery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kitchener Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Kitchener Street and Wellesley Street East (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/154430110: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Auckland Art Gallery' (119 m across).
notes: New Zealand's largest art gallery, with a distinctive kauri-canopy extension.

text.description:
Auckland Art Gallery (Toi o Tāmaki) is the city's main public gallery, and it sits just below the hilltop of Albert Park in the central city. The original building dates from 1888, which makes it the first permanent art gallery in New Zealand. It began life sharing its walls with the public library. The stone château-style building, with its arched windows, is the part most visitors want to photograph. Next to it is a modern timber-and-glass extension, so a single walk around the block gives you two very different looks.

The collection now runs to more than 18,000 artworks, but you don't need to go inside to get a good picture. The strongest phone shot is the corner view of the original building from Kitchener Street. The old stone, the arched windows and the city street around them tell the story in one frame. If you want the entrance, walk up towards the front door and shoot the whole building with its canopy in the foreground. For a different angle, go up into Albert Park and look down on the east sculpture terrace and the new extension. Sculptures in the courtyard change regularly, so what you see may differ from pictures online. Exterior viewpoints are the safer choice, as flash and tripods are discouraged inside.
text.geographic_location: In the central city of Auckland, set just below the hilltop Albert Park. The original stone building can be seen from its corner on Kitchener Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Albert Park in central Auckland. The gallery sits at the foot of the park, on its downhill side. Check a local journey planner for stations or stops before you set out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement or traffic stops you stepping back far enough to get the whole facade in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Kitchener Street and Wellesley Street East (corner of the original building). The corner view of the original stone building with its arched windows, framed against the city street. Look east towards the gallery.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the corner of the building up with one of the vertical lines, so the stonework doesn't lean. Keep the arched windows in the upper two-thirds of the frame, with a little street in front for scale. As an alternative, walk up to the entrance for the full 1888 building with its canopy in the foreground. Or go to Albert Park for the sculpture terrace and the modern extension from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Hold the phone level, and don't tilt it upwards, or the building will look as if it is falling backwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the facade is evenly lit and there is not much traffic in the street. Soft daylight is kinder to the stonework than hard midday sun.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the street, but check the official site before you go for gallery access and any rules about photography inside.

name: Auckland Domain
label: Auckland Domain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Domain Wintergardens' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Domain Wintergardens' (relation/8280142): middle (62 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/6029919: large area 'Auckland Domain' (1528 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Auckland's oldest park, on an extinct volcano, with the Wintergardens.

text.description:
Auckland Domain is the city's oldest park, 75 hectares of lawns, sports fields, old trees and ponds in the suburb of Grafton. It also sits inside the remains of a volcano, Pukekawa, which erupted about 100,000 years ago. The park's Māori name is Pukekawa, and today it is officially called Pukekawa / Auckland Domain. The Auckland War Memorial Museum stands on the old crater rim, and a small cone called Pukekaroa Hill rises in the middle. Because the park is so big, the best phone photo here is a single scene rather than the whole place.

The most photogenic scene is the Domain Wintergardens courtyard, between two large glasshouses on the north side of Pukekaroa Hill. A formal pond, marble statues and the glasshouse domes make a tidy, symmetrical picture, and the glass roofs catch the light well. Photography is fine in the courtyard and other public areas, but it can be restricted inside the glasshouses, so keep your shots outside unless a sign says otherwise.

If you have time for a second picture, the museum's columned front looks good from the grounds. Grafton Bridge is also suggested for a view across the park's trees towards the city.
text.geographic_location: Auckland Domain lies in the central suburb of Grafton, on the hill between Parnell and Grafton and close to the middle of Auckland. The Wintergardens are on the north side of the park's central hill, Pukekaroa.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Domain is in the central suburb of Grafton, and the Wintergardens are on the north side of the park's central hill. Use the map and signs in the park to find the Wintergardens courtyard. Check the official site before you go for current Wintergardens opening times. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole courtyard, pond and both glasshouses into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the statues and pond. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a statue against the glass domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Domain Wintergardens (central courtyard between the two glasshouses). The formal courtyard with its pond, marble statues and glasshouse domes framing the subject, with the glasshouses behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the pond up with the centre of the frame so the two glasshouses balance on either side. Crouch slightly so a statue stands against the glass rather than the sky. For a different view, try the museum's columned front from the grounds, or Grafton Bridge for a view over the park's trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glasshouse roof to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright glass does not wash out. Keep your phone steady and check for reflections before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light is soft and fewer people are about. Light hitting the glass roofs is also a good moment.

text.access_note: The courtyard and public areas of the Domain can be photographed, but photography inside the glasshouses is sometimes restricted, so check the official site before you go for current opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Reflections on glass can spoil a phone photo, so check the frame before shooting.

name: New Zealand Maritime Museum
label: Maritime Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quay Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Quay Street and Hobson Street (our map tiles).

notes: Waterfront museum of sailing and seafaring history.

text.description: The New Zealand Maritime Museum sits on Hobson Wharf on the Auckland waterfront, right beside the Viaduct Harbour. It tells the story of New Zealand and the sea, from the first Polynesian voyagers to the America's Cup. For a phone photo, the best part is the entrance. It folds the Launchman's Building, built in 1920 and given a Category II heritage listing in 1981, into the modern museum. That gives you old and new in one frame, with the harbour behind. The museum opened in August 1993, and its building won an Auckland Architecture Award in 2010. Outside the entrance stands KZ1, a yacht built for the 1988 America's Cup and given to the museum in 1990, which makes a good foreground subject. From the corner on Quay Street you get a straight-on view of the entrance block and its old facade. If you have time, walk out onto Hobson Wharf too. From there you can photograph the museum with the waka Haunui and the water beside it. Wide, simple compositions work best here, because the buildings are large and the pavement is open. Take a few frames from different spots and compare them.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on Hobson Wharf on the Auckland waterfront in central Auckland. It sits next to the Viaduct Harbour (Viaduct Basin) and Princes Wharf.
text.directions_text: Head for the Viaduct Harbour area on the central Auckland waterfront. From there the museum building lies to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole entrance block and some harbour into the frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the old facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Quay Street and Hobson Street (corner at the museum entrance). The museum's entrance block, including the 1920 Launchman's Building facade, with the harbour frontage behind it. Face north-west towards the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the facade with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Keep the old Launchman's Building on one side and the newer museum structure on the other. KZ1 by the entrance can go in the foreground if it is in view. For a second view, walk out to Hobson Wharf and photograph the museum with the waka Haunui and the harbour beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its colour. Hold the phone level and keep the ultra-wide shots away from the edges of the frame, where lines can bend.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight works best, especially softer morning or late-afternoon light, when the facade is evenly lit. Weekdays and early hours are often quieter on the waterfront.

text.access_note: The outside of the museum and the waterfront are public space, but entry to the museum itself and any rules for photography inside may vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer morning or late-afternoon light is generally kinder to building facades than harsh midday sun.
The waterfront is often quieter on weekday mornings.
KZ1 may be visible near the entrance and can work as a foreground subject.
Ultra-wide lenses can bend straight lines near the edges of the frame.

name: Queen Street, Auckland
label: Queen Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen Street and Victoria Street intersection' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Queen Street and Victoria Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14149237: large area 'Queen Street' (1699 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The main street, running from the waterfront up the central city.

text.description: Queen Street is the main commercial street of Auckland's city centre, and it is easiest to photograph as one long, straight view. It was named after Queen Victoria and was an early part of the town founded in 1840. In 1902 it became the first asphalted street in New Zealand, and electric trams ran along it until 1956. The street is almost three kilometres long and close to straight, so a view down its length holds together well in a phone frame. It also has very high foot traffic, which gives plenty of life but means you should work quickly and keep out of people's way. The footpaths were widened and relaid in a 2006-2008 upgrade, with new trees such as liquidambars and Nīkau palms, and these make a useful leafy foreground. Keep your phone level and let the buildings lead the eye down the street. If you want a second angle, Aotea Square, near the top of the street, may offer a view back along it (check on the day), and Queen Street near Farmers gives a view with the Sky Tower at the far end.
text.geographic_location: Queen Street runs through the middle of Auckland's city centre, from Te Komititanga square on the waterfront (next to Waitematā railway station and Commercial Bay) south-southwest towards Karangahape Road. The photo spot is at the corner where Victoria Street meets Queen Street.
text.directions_text: Start at Te Komititanga square on the waterfront, next to Waitematā railway station, and head south up Queen Street towards the Victoria Street corner. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the long view down the street. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pack the buildings closer together, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the street and the buildings above it in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Queen Street and Victoria Street (corner where Victoria Street meets Queen Street; sources name both the West and East sides). Looking south down the length of Queen Street from the corner, with the street's buildings receding toward the harbour. Either side of Victoria Street can work, so pick the corner with the clearest view on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame so the buildings on each side lean in evenly. Keep the phone level so the verticals stay straight, and include a few people on the footpath for scale. For a different view, try Aotea Square (which may offer a view back along the street) or Queen Street near Farmers (with the Sky Tower at the end).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo to catch moving people, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, and softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the building fronts. Whenever you go, wait for a gap in the people and traffic and keep to the footpath.

text.access_note: Queen Street is an open public street, but check the official site before you go for any road works, closures or pedestrian-only changes.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually calmer on Queen Street than the middle of the day.
Softer morning or late-afternoon light is generally kinder to street photographs than midday sun.
Traffic and pedestrians are likely to be in the frame at the corner of Victoria Street and Queen Street, so take care on the footpath.
Aotea Square may offer a view back along Queen Street; check on the day.

name: Auckland Town Hall
label: Auckland Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Aotea Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Aotea Square' (relation/11846232): middle (244 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23904006: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Auckland Town Hall' (123 m across).
notes: Edwardian Baroque civic hall with a landmark clock tower.

text.description: Auckland Town Hall is an Edwardian landmark on Queen Street, at the corner with Greys Avenue. It was designed by the Melbourne architects JJ & EJ Clark and opened on 14 December 1911. The five-storey building has a 40-metre clock tower, pale Oamaru limestone on the upper floors and a dark, heavily textured stone base. That two-tone stonework gives a phone camera plenty to work with. Inside, the Great Hall seats 1,673 people and houses the country's largest organ, but from outside you are photographing the facade and tower. The easiest place for a clean, open shot is Aotea Square. Start wide to take in the whole front, then zoom in on the clock and the stonework. Keep the tower upright with the gridlines on. If you want a second angle, the Queen Street footpath gives a straighter view of the street front. Aotea Square is often used for events, so stalls or stages may sometimes get in the way. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the pale stone.
text.geographic_location: In the Auckland CBD, on Queen Street at the corner of Greys Avenue, with Aotea Square just to its north.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Aotea Square from anywhere along Queen Street in the Auckland CBD. If you are coming from further out, navigate to Aotea Square or Auckland Town Hall on Queen Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and clock tower together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the tower gets cut off, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Aotea Square. The Town Hall's neo-Baroque facade and clock tower rising across the open paved plaza, with the square in the foreground. For a different angle, the footpath on the Queen Street side shows the full street front and the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep a strip of the paved square at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of space. Wait for people to cross if you want a clean foreground, or let a few stay in for scale. Then step in and zoom to the clock face and the contrast between the dark base and the pale upper storeys.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the limestone and the sky keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold your phone against something steady, such as your own raised elbows, for sharper results.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the facade. Check the square for festival set-ups or closures on the day.

text.access_note: Aotea Square is an open public space and the building's exterior can be photographed from the street, but the interior needs an event or tour, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone's gridlines on helps keep the tower upright in the frame.
Ultra-wide shots taken from close range can make tall buildings appear to lean.
The Town Hall may be lit at night, which would suit night mode, but check on the evening.

name: Aotea Square
label: Aotea Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Queen Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11846232: 'Sir Dove-Myer Robinson', the best-known feature inside 'Aotea Square' (244 m across).
notes: Central civic square with the Waharoa gateway and regular events.

text.description: Aotea Square is a big, open paved square in the middle of Auckland's city centre, and it is easiest to photograph from the Queen Street entrance. There, a carved gateway called Waharoa stands in the foreground and the square opens out behind it. The gateway is by Māori sculptor Selwyn Muru, made in wood and copper. It is a modern take on a traditional entry gate, with birds, fish, a crescent moon and stars among its symbols. That gives your picture an immediate point of interest and a sense of place. The square opened in 1979 and was redeveloped, finishing in November 2010. It is now designed to hold crowds of up to 20,000 people for concerts, markets and gatherings. The Edwardian Auckland Town Hall is at the Queen Street end, and the Aotea Centre lies on the western side. There is also a bronze statue of former mayor Sir Dove-Myer Robinson in front of the Town Hall, which makes a good second subject. For a different view, turn round and photograph the square with the Town Hall rising behind it. You can also look up for the floating Neil Dawson sculpture, Mountains and Valleys, against the sky or the surrounding buildings. Because it is a gathering place, expect people to wander through your frame. Use them to show scale, or come when it is quieter. Temporary light installations and events change what you will see, so check what is on before you visit.
text.geographic_location: Aotea Square is in the heart of Auckland's city centre (the CBD), next to Queen Street. It lies beside the Town Hall, with the Aotea Centre on its western side.
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or tram stop for this spot, so head for Queen Street in the city centre. From Queen Street, look for the carved Waharoa gateway at the entrance to the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the gateway and the open square into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statue or for carved details on the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Queen Street (at the Waharoa gateway entrance, looking west into the square). The Waharoa gateway in the foreground with the open paved square stretching away behind it. The statue of Sir Dove-Myer Robinson is ahead of you in that direction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the gateway in the foreground and let the square lead the eye into the distance. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the buildings do not lean. For a second picture, walk into the square and turn round to catch the Town Hall behind the open space. You can also point the phone upwards for the Mountains and Valleys sculpture against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gateway to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the carving keeps its detail. Gridlines help keep the verticals straight. Try a Live Photo if people are moving through the scene, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Come when it is quieter if you want fewer people crossing your frame.

text.access_note: Aotea Square is an open public square, but events can change what is on show, so check the official site before you go.

name: Civic Theatre (Auckland)
label: Civic Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen Street & Wellesley Street' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Queen Street and Wellesley Street West (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23906749: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Civic' (92 m across).
notes: Atmospheric 1929 theatre with an ornate facade and interior.

text.description:
The Civic is Auckland's grand old theatre, opened on 20 December 1929 and now a performing-arts venue, live-music space and cinema seating 2,378 people. It was built in the 'atmospheric' style, where the auditorium is designed to feel like an open-air garden under a night sky with twinkling stars. It is the largest surviving atmospheric cinema in Australasia. It was reopened in 1999 after a major two-year restoration, and its interior also appeared in Peter Jackson's 2005 film King Kong. The foyer has an Indian-inspired look, with seated Buddhas, twisted columns and domed ceilings.

For a phone photo, the best-value shot is from outside, at street level. It is a busy city corner, so expect people and traffic in the frame. Wait for a gap, or let a few passers-by add a sense of scale. For a second angle, Aotea Square is another recommended viewpoint for the facade, showing it across the open paved space, with public art and city life in the foreground. Inside, the foyer is the showpiece, but the interior is only open with a ticket or at set times, and photography rules vary, so ask staff or check the venue's rules first.
text.geographic_location: The Civic is in central Auckland, on Queen Street at the corner of Wellesley Street. Aotea Square is another recommended viewpoint for the facade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Auckland city centre and walk to the corner of Queen Street and Wellesley Street, outside the main entrance. Aotea Square is another recommended viewpoint for the facade if you want a second angle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner facade and entrance. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building will not fit from the pavement. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the upper facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Queen Street and Wellesley Street West (corner outside the main entrance). The theatre's corner facade and main entry, framed by the Queen Street and Wellesley Street frontages.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the corner of the building with one of the vertical lines to keep the walls from leaning. Keep the phone level and step back as far as is safe. If you have time, try Aotea Square as an alternative, where the facade sits across the open paved space.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright so the detail on the building holds up. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Crowd levels at this corner can vary, so simply wait for a gap in the foot traffic. Evening can add lit-up shopfronts and a show crowd, but check what is on first.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public street, but the interior is ticketed or open only at set times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ferry Building, Auckland
label: Ferry Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queens Wharf' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Queens Wharf' (node/8246011891): point.

text.description:
The Ferry Building sits on Auckland's waterfront at the harbour end of the city centre, and it is a recognisable subject on the shoreline. The best-supported view is from Queens Wharf, the pier just along the waterfront. From there the Ferry Building appears in the foreground or middle distance, with the water and the modern Cloud building beside it. The old and new buildings together give you a good sense of the waterfront in a single frame.

Heritage New Zealand has a photo set showing the building framed from Queens Wharf, and a visitor guide lists the wharf as a free place for harbour and waterfront photos. If you would rather see the building square-on, the top of Queen Street, where it meets the waterfront, shows the façade head-on. It is a good second picture.

On your phone, take a wide shot first so the building, the water and the Cloud all fit. Then step closer or zoom in for a tighter picture of the façade. Keep the gridlines on so the building stands straight. Work has been reported around the building in the past, which can get in the way of clean photos, so check current conditions when you arrive. If a barrier or crane spoils one angle, move a few steps along the wharf and try again.
text.geographic_location: On Auckland's central waterfront, where Queen Street meets the harbour. The Ferry Building stands next to the modern Cloud building, with Queens Wharf close by.
text.directions_text: Head to Auckland's city-centre waterfront and walk down to the harbour from the top of Queen Street. From there the Ferry Building is to the south-west, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the Ferry Building, the water and the Cloud building in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the building will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Queens Wharf. The Ferry Building in the foreground or middle distance, with the waterfront and the modern Cloud building beside it in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Include a strip of water or waterfront in front so the building sits in its setting. For a different view, walk to the top of Queen Street where it meets the waterfront and photograph the façade head-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the façade does not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and keep the lens clean, as sea air can leave a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the early morning or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer. Check the site conditions on the day too, as construction work has been reported nearby.

text.access_note: Queens Wharf is listed as a free place for waterfront photos, but check current conditions around the building when you arrive.

Sea air can leave a film on a phone lens, so wiping it helps.
Gridlines help keep a building's vertical lines straight.

name: Albert Park, Auckland
label: Albert Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Albert Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Albert Park' (relation/9636962): middle (571 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9636962: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Albert Park' (573 m across).
notes: Historic city park with a rotunda, fountains and a clock tower.

text.description:
Albert Park is a public park on a rise in central Auckland, right beside the University of Auckland. Its formal layout of paths and flower gardens has changed little since the 1880s, so it still feels like a Victorian town park. The centrepiece is a large cast iron fountain, imported from Great Britain in 1881. Dolphins ridden by cherubs blow horns that spout water, and a figure of Aphrodite stands on top. That makes a tidy, classic subject for a phone photo.

Some of the trees date from the 1800s, and more than 80 species were planted here between 1874 and 1908. The paths and benches around the fountain give you natural lines to lead the eye in.

A statue of Queen Victoria (1897) stands to the north of the fountain, and the bandstand (built 1900–01) is to the south. If you want a second picture, the bandstand in the foreground can have the Sky Tower rising behind the trees, depending on where you stand. In autumn, Princes Street has an avenue of ginkgo trees with the university clock tower behind, which is quieter than the central lawns.

Keep your lens clean, check for people walking through before you tap the shutter, and take a few frames at different heights.
text.geographic_location: Albert Park is in central Auckland, on rising ground between Wellesley Street East and Princes Street, next to the University of Auckland and the Auckland Art Gallery. The fountain is in the flat central area at the top of the park.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so approach on foot from the University of Auckland or the Wellesley Street East side of central Auckland. Enter by any of the park gates and follow the sealed paths uphill to the flat central area, where the fountain stands. The path from the Bowen Avenue and Kitchener Street corner climbs steeply, so allow a little extra time if you take that way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the fountain with flowerbeds and trees around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the whole formal layout, and try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the dolphins, cherubs and Aphrodite figure.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Albert Park (central area beside the Victorian fountain). The Victorian fountain framed by flowerbeds and mature trees, with the park's paths and benches around it. From here the park's middle lies a little to the east, and the fountain, flowerbeds, mature trees, paths and benches all fall into view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on the centre line, with a curve of path or a flowerbed in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the fountain and trees don't lean. For a second shot, go to the bandstand and frame it low with the Sky Tower behind. Whether the tower shows depends on your angle, so shift a few steps until it appears. In autumn, Princes Street is a quieter spot for the ginkgo avenue and the clock tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and water don't burn out. Try a Live Photo to catch the water moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and lights the fountain well. Flowerbeds add colour in spring and summer, and cherry blossom and magnolias bloom in spring.

text.access_note: Albert Park is an open public park and free to enter; check the official Auckland Council site before you go if you need details on any works or closures.

name: Holy Trinity Cathedral, Auckland
label: Holy Trinity Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parnell Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Parnell Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23907448: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holy Trinity Cathedral' (92 m across).
notes: Modern Anglican cathedral in Parnell with a striking stained-glass window.

text.description:
Holy Trinity Cathedral is the mother church of the Anglican Diocese of Auckland, in the residential suburb of Parnell. It is a building of two halves. The older brick and reinforced-concrete neo-Gothic chancel was joined by a modern nave designed by architect Professor Richard Toy. The foundation stone was laid in 1957, and the main church was consecrated in 1973. That mix of old and new is what makes it interesting to photograph: steep gables, a large entrance window and plain modern lines sit together in one frame.

This is the clearest exterior view of the gabled façade and its big window. Beside the cathedral stands the wooden Gothic Revival St Mary's Church, designed by Benjamin Mountfort and finished in 1897. It was moved across Parnell Road to its present spot in 1982, so you may catch it at the edge of a wider shot.

The cathedral is still a working church, so be considerate of anyone coming and going. For a second angle, walk round to St Stephens Avenue, where the red-brick chancel and the modern nave fit into one frame.
text.geographic_location: In Parnell, a residential suburb of Auckland, on Parnell Road. St Mary's Church, the former cathedral, stands right beside it.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for Parnell Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on view of the west front. If a passer-by or the width of the footpath stops you fitting the whole façade in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). If you want to pick out details such as the gable or the window, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Parnell Road (footpath in front of the west façade, near the entrance). The west front of the cathedral, with the large entrance window and the gabled façade seen straight on. The cathedral lies to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the façade up with them, so the walls don't lean. Keep the entrance window in the centre of the frame, with a little sky above the gable. For a second view, try St Stephens Avenue, which shows the red-brick chancel and the modern nave and gables together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the brick and concrete keep their detail. Hold the phone level and still, and take a few shots to pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with soft, even light so the façade has no harsh shadows. Late afternoon may suit the west front best. Early in the morning or on a quieter day there should be fewer people on the footpath.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public footpath, but the cathedral is a working church, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Parnell Rose Gardens
label: Parnell Rose Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fred Ambler Lookout' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fred Ambler Lookout' (node/8813321418): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/43435523: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parnell Rose Garden' (177 m across).
notes: Harbour-view rose gardens in Parnell.

text.description:
Parnell Rose Gardens is the everyday name for Dove-Myer Robinson Park, a park of several hectares in Parnell, named after Auckland's longest-serving mayor, who held the post for 18 years. More than 5,000 roses grow here, laid out in beds along gentle paths, and the 'white garden' is a popular spot for wedding photos. The Nancy Steen Garden, opened in 1984, shows older heritage roses and has a softer, cottage-style look than the neat modern beds. The old timber house that is now the Luxerose cafe dates from around 1905 and gives the grounds a pleasant period backdrop.

The park works for photos because you get close flower detail and a big view in one short visit. From the Fred Ambler Lookout at the lower end of the park, you look over the harbour to the Auckland skyline, with the container terminal below. Then it is a short stroll back up to the rose beds. The best flowers are usually from November, when the Parnell Festival of Roses is held, and into the new year. Outside those months the beds are quieter, but the views stay the same.

On your phone, treat it as two jobs: a wide skyline shot at the lookout, then close-ups among the roses. Some reviewers find the rose garden small, so you will not need long. Dogs must be kept on a lead.
text.geographic_location: In Parnell, on the slope above Auckland's harbour, in Dove-Myer Robinson Park next to the Parnell rose beds. The park looks across towards the city centre skyline.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a journey planner for the best way to reach Dove-Myer Robinson Park from the centre of Parnell. Walk through the rose garden to the Fred Ambler Lookout at the lower end of the park. Between the lookout and the middle of the rose beds it is a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: At the lookout, start on the ultra-wide (0.5x) or panorama for the full harbour and skyline. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the view with the terminal in the foreground, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the city towers. In the rose beds, use the default lens (1x) for whole-bed shots and the telephoto for single blooms.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Fred Ambler Lookout (lookout at the lower end of Dove-Myer Robinson Park, reached from the garden). A panorama of the harbour and the Auckland CBD skyline, with the container terminal below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the skyline along the upper third, with the harbour and terminal filling the lower part. Keep the phone level so the water line stays straight. For roses, get low and close, and keep the bed in soft focus behind one bloom. If you want an alternative, try the White Garden, where pale roses sit along the paths with the harbour and city beyond. The Nancy Steen Garden has old-fashioned roses mixed with other plants and is usually quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the skyline to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour. For close-ups, tap the flower itself, and use portrait mode on a single rose for a softer background. Live Photos can help if the breeze moves the blooms.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, after about 17:00, tends to give softer light for both the roses and the view. Mornings are usually calmer if you want fewer people in your shots. Bloom is best from November into the new year.

text.access_note: This is a public park, but the opening times are not clear, so check the official council page before you go; dogs must be kept on a lead.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon (after about 17:00) tends to give softer light.
Mornings are usually quieter, with fewer visitors.
Roses are usually at their best from November into the new year, although the exact peak varies.
The park is a public space with no entry charge.

name: St Patrick's Cathedral, Auckland
label: St Patrick's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Saint Patrick's Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Saint Patrick's Square' (relation/16691367): middle (151 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23919629: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Patrick’s Cathedral' (69 m across).
notes: Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral beside the Sky Tower.

text.description:
St Patrick's Cathedral is the Catholic cathedral of Auckland, on the corner of Federal Street and Wyndham Street in the middle of the city. That is why it works well for a phone photo: the stonework and spires fill the frame without crowding.

The church has a long history on this site. The land was granted to Bishop Pompallier, New Zealand's first Catholic bishop, in 1841. A wooden chapel opened in 1843 and a stone church followed in the late 1840s. The building you see today was finished in 1907 and opened on 23 February 1908. It is a Category I historic place, registered by Heritage New Zealand in 1984. Its spire also appears in the 1988 film The Navigator: A Medieval Odyssey.

From here the building and spire sit neatly framed by the open space. For the view of the west-facade entrance from Saint Patrick's Square, walk round the building. For another angle, walk along Wyndham Street toward the cathedral and shoot the facade and tower as they come into view. After dark, the corner of Hobson Street is a good spot to see the cathedral lit up, with the presbytery in the foreground. Check on the day.

This is a working place of worship. Photography outside is generally fine, but keep voices low and avoid flash if you step inside.
text.geographic_location: St Patrick's Cathedral is in the Auckland CBD, on the corner of Federal Street and Wyndham Street. Saint Patrick's Square lies in front of its west facade, which you reach by walking round the building.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Auckland CBD, then walk or go by taxi or hired scooter to the corner of Federal Street and Wyndham Street. Look for the spire, which stands out above the surrounding streets. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full building and spire in from where you stand. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire, the stonework and the tower seen from Wyndham Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Saint Patrick's Square (in front of the main (west) facade, facing the entrance). The full Gothic Revival facade and spires of the cathedral, framed by the open square in front. From here you see the Gothic Revival building and spire framed by the open space. For the square and the west-facade entrance view, walk round the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central axis of the building with the middle line so the spires look balanced. Hold the phone level, as tilting it up makes the towers lean inward. Keep a strip of foreground at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. For a different view, walk along Wyndham Street and shoot the facade and tower as you approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pale stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't wash out. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady. Avoid flash near the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the full building. After dark, the lit cathedral is worth a try from the Hobson Street corner.

text.access_note: The square and streets around the cathedral are public, but the cathedral is a place of worship: keep quiet during Mass, avoid flash, and check the official site for Mass and visiting times before you go.
